speaker_role: independent counselor/test-prep marketer (SupertutorTV, ~20 years of admissions consulting experience)
commercial_incentive: yes - SupertutorTV sells essay consulting, private tutoring, and test-prep courses, promoted at both start and end
key_insights: Blended overall admit rates are described as misleading because they combine very different early-round and regular-round admit rates (e.g., an 11% overall rate can mask a 20% early rate and 3% regular rate).

Presents tiers of schools by early-vs-regular admission-rate multiplier, citing schools like Tulane, Grinnell, Columbia, and Dartmouth as having 4x-8x+ early advantages, and many top-10-ish schools (Northwestern, Brown, Cornell, Duke, Harvard, Yale, Penn) in a 3x-4x tier.

Cautions that at schools like Penn or Harvard, part of the apparent ED/REA boost is attributable to legacy and athletic recruits, who are often instructed to apply early, so the real advantage for other applicants may be smaller than the raw multiplier suggests.

Notes many selective schools fill 50% or more (some 60-80%+) of their incoming class through early rounds (ED/REA), which the speaker treats as strong evidence in favor of applying early when feasible.

Advises using a college's net price calculator (and crowd-sourced data from forums/Facebook groups) to estimate real cost before committing to Early Decision, since ED offers can't be compared against other schools' aid.

States a student can be released from an Early Decision commitment if the school's financial aid offer is genuinely insufficient, illustrated with an anecdote of an international student who successfully petitioned for more aid rather than withdrawing.

Suggests students from underrepresented or lower-income backgrounds who can't realistically commit to a binding ED round are still given consideration in regular decision and shouldn't feel they've lost their shot.
Notes some schools (e.g., Howard, Baylor, University of Denver cited as examples) show little to no early-application admit-rate advantage, so the strategy doesn't apply uniformly everywhere.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Columbia early admit rate ~12.5% vs. regular ~2.7%, a 4.6x difference, with 53.7% of the class filled via early admits (per SupertutorTV's data analysis)
Dartmouth early decision admit rate cited at 21.3%, described as the highest Ivy League admit rate (per SupertutorTV)
Notre Dame fills about 82.2% of its class via restrictive early action, though its early-vs-regular admit rate advantage is only about 1.7x (per SupertutorTV)
notable_or_distinctive: Goes beyond generic ED/EA definitions to rank specific named colleges by their actual early-vs-regular admit-rate multiplier and percent of class filled early, explicitly flagging legacy/athlete distortion in the numbers.
reliability_notes: Figures are presented as pulled from Common Data Set-type sources but are not individually cited with dates in the transcript, so exact numbers should be re-verified against current Common Data Sets; content is delivered by a paid consulting business with a financial interest in early-application anxiety.
